785.title: Trent on scripture
785.hook: the council confirms the full canon, and scripture with tradition
785.howItsDone: Catholic Bibles print the deuterocanonical books among the others, and readings from them, like Wisdom 3 at funerals, are part of the Mass lectionary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Catholic Reformation began at Trent. Your line was reform from within.

"But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them." It's among the readings the Church offers for funerals, from the Book of Wisdom. Open some Bibles and you won't find it at all. Open others and it's there, in a section set apart. In a Catholic Bible it sits among the other books, no fence around it. Which books belong in the Bible was one of the reformers' questions, and Trent answered it early.
screen: `A FUNERAL READING.` → `IN SOME BIBLES, NOT OTHERS.` → `TRENT ANSWERS EARLY.`

segments.voice: First, the list. The council didn't just say the Bible matters; it wrote out the books by name, one after another, so nobody could wonder. Among them are Tobias, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, also called Sirach, Baruch, and the books of the Maccabees. Catholics call these the deuterocanonical books. The decree speaks of them as books the Church was accustomed to read; Trent made the list official and binding. Next, scripture with tradition. The decree says the truth and discipline of the Gospel are found in the written books and in the unwritten traditions that came from Christ through the apostles, and the council receives both with the same reverence. Not the Bible versus the Church, but the Bible read inside a living Church. Then, where others stand, without ranking. Protestant traditions call these same books the Apocrypha. Some Protestant Bibles print them in a separate section, as useful reading; others leave them out. Orthodox Bibles include them as well. The disagreement is real, and it's an honest one about how the early Church read. Last, the Latin. Trent also named the old Latin Bible, the Vulgate, as the authentic text for public reading and teaching, and called for it to be carefully printed. The council's point was to name every book the Church reads, each one in full standing.
screen: `THE BOOKS LISTED BY NAME.` · `SCRIPTURE AND TRADITION, TOGETHER.` · `OTHER CHURCHES, OTHER LISTS.` · `THE VULGATE NAMED AUTHENTIC.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE CANON.`

segments.voice: If you have a Catholic Bible, open to Wisdom, chapter three, or to Sirach or Tobias, and read a few verses slowly, out loud if you can; if not, stay with today's line: the souls of the just are in the hand of God. Let one name come to mind, someone you've lost. If you pray, place them, in your mind, in that hand.
Vulgate. The old Latin Bible that Trent named as the Church's authentic text, standing alongside the full list of books it declared canonical. Today's word.
Your line: the whole canon. A list written out by name, so nobody had to wonder. See you tomorrow.

786.title: Trent on grace
786.hook: justification begins with grace, received in faith, and bears fruit in works
786.howItsDone: Catholics are taught that justification begins with God's grace, given in baptism, received in faith and growing through love and good works; the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation have signed a joint declaration on the doctrine of justification.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vulgate, and the books listed by name. Your line was the whole canon.

Two lines, one Bible. Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims, "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." James writes, "faith without works is dead." Read either one alone and it can sound like the whole story. The reformers leaned hard on Paul, and some of them were uneasy with James. At Trent, the bishops spent a long time trying to hold both lines in one hand.
screen: `PAUL: BY GRACE, THROUGH FAITH.` → `JAMES: FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD.` → `BOTH IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: The council's decree on justification, being made right with God, moves in a careful order. First, grace begins it. The beginning, it says, comes from God's grace, which goes ahead of us and calls us without any merit of our own. We don't start the journey; God does. Second, faith receives it. The decree calls faith the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification. And it adds a striking line: nothing that comes before justification, neither faith nor works, earns the grace of justification. It's a gift. Third, it bears fruit. For Trent, justification isn't only having sins forgiven; it's being made new on the inside. A person made new grows, and that growth shows in love and in works. That's where James comes in: works aren't the price of grace. They're what grace does when it's alive in someone. Then, the guardrail. Among its canons, the council condemned the idea that a person can be made right with God by their own works, without God's grace through Christ. Some people imagine Catholics believe you earn your way to God. Trent rules that out: good works matter, but they grow from grace, never apart from it. Catholics and Lutherans still differ on how this works in a person. But the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation have since signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification by grace.
screen: `FIRST: GRACE GOES AHEAD.` · `SECOND: FAITH, THE ROOT.` · `THIRD: GRACE BEARS FRUIT.` · `NO ONE EARNS IT BY WORKS.` · then, large: `GRACE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three good things in your life you didn't earn: a meal someone else cooked, someone who loved you before you'd done anything, a morning you were given. Let each one sit for a few breaths and just receive it, without turning it into a to-do list. If you pray, say thank you, simply, once for each; if you don't, just notice them.
Justification. Trent's teaching that being made right with God begins with grace, is received in faith, and bears fruit in works. Today's word.
Your line: grace first. The gift comes before any good we do. Day seven hundred eighty-six, done.

787.title: Trent's reforms
787.hook: seminaries, a catechism, and a Mass book that lasted four hundred years
787.howItsDone: Catholic parishes pray for vocations, often in the Prayer of the Faithful at Mass, and dioceses keep or share a seminary where future priests live and study before ordination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justification. Your line was grace first: God moves before we do. Trent wrote that down; the harder question was how to get it into a parish.

A decree is only ink until somebody carries it out. The bishops at Trent could settle grace and scripture on paper, but a village priest who had never been trained would still stand at the altar on Sunday and do what he had always done. So the council turned from doctrine to plumbing. Who teaches the priests? What book do they teach from? Which words does the Mass use? Today's word is the name that stuck to the answers: Tridentine.
screen: `INK UNTIL SOMEONE ACTS.` → `WHO TEACHES THE PRIESTS?` → `TRIDENTINE.`

segments.voice: Tridentine simply means: of Trent. It got attached to three things. First, the seminary. Trent asked each diocese to keep a college where boys and young men preparing for the priesthood would live, pray and study together, learning scripture, the sacraments and how to care for souls. Formation became a place with a timetable. Second, the catechism. The council called for a book that pastors could teach from, and after it closed, one was published in Rome: the Roman Catechism, sometimes called the Catechism of the Council of Trent. It was written for priests, so that what they preached on Sunday matched what the council had taught. Third, the Missal. The council left the reform of the Mass book to the pope, and Pope Pius the Fifth issued a Roman Missal for the Latin Church. That Mass, in Latin, is what people mean today by the Tridentine Mass. Four hundred years is the round number people give for how long the book shaped the Sunday of Latin Catholics, until the reforms after the Second Vatican Council. Some Catholics still celebrate it, and the Church has set rules for when and where. Underneath all three is one idea. Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims, "The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few." Trent's answer was not only to pray for laborers, but to train them.

If you pray, use the line Jesus gave right after the one about the harvest: "Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth labourers into his harvest." If you don't pray, simply wish them good teachers.

788.title: Vatican I, 1870
788.hook: the pope is protected from error only when solemnly defining faith or morals for the whole Church, rarely used
788.howItsDone: Catholics distinguish a pope's solemn definitions, which the Church holds as infallible, from his ordinary teaching, homilies and personal opinions, and Catholic catechisms explain the narrow conditions set by the First Vatican Council.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tridentine: of Trent, the seminaries, the catechism and the Mass book. Your line was four hundred years. Now, a jump to the next council, held at the Vatican itself.

A pope says he likes a film. A pope gives an interview on a plane. A pope picks a soccer team. Somewhere, within the hour, a headline asks whether Catholics now have to agree with him. The question comes from a word the First Vatican Council defined, and it's often misheard. It doesn't mean the pope is never wrong. It means something much smaller and much stranger. Today's word: infallibility.
screen: `A POPE ON A PLANE.` → `DO CATHOLICS HAVE TO AGREE?` → `INFALLIBILITY.`

segments.voice: Start with what it isn't. Infallibility is not sinlessness; popes go to confession too. It isn't about a pope's opinions, his homilies, his interviews or his politics either. Now, what the council actually said. Its constitution on the papacy, called Pastor Aeternus, teaches that when the Roman Pontiff speaks ex cathedra, from the chair, meaning when, as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, he defines a teaching on faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he is kept from error by the help God promised to Peter. Every one of those conditions has to be there. Next, the reason given. The council pointed to Jesus's words at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and thou, being once converted, confirm thy brethren." And the same document says the Holy Spirit was not promised so the popes could make known new teaching, but so they could guard and faithfully explain what was handed down. A guardrail, not an engine. Finally, how often. Catholic teachers point out that solemn definitions like this are rare; the example people usually give is Pope Pius the Twelfth defining Mary's Assumption. Other Christians, Orthodox and Protestant, do not accept this teaching, and some Catholics at the council itself argued that defining it was unwise.
screen: `NOT SINLESSNESS, NOT OPINIONS.` · `EX CATHEDRA: FAITH OR MORALS, FOR ALL.` · `CONFIRM THY BRETHREN.` · `A GUARDRAIL, NOT AN ENGINE.` · then, large: `RARER THAN PEOPLE THINK.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly through the conditions, one per breath: the pope, speaking as teacher of all Christians, defining, faith or morals, for the whole Church. Then let go of everything that falls outside them: the interviews, the opinions, the plane rides. If you pray, pray for the pope in Jesus's words, that his faith fail not.
Infallibility. Protection from error when the pope solemnly defines faith or morals for the whole Church; not sinlessness, and not his every word. Today's word.
Your line: rarer than people think. All five conditions at once, or it isn't this. See you tomorrow.

789.title: Faith and reason, 1870
789.hook: God can be known by reason from created things
789.howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that God can be known by reason from the created world and also through revelation, and Catholic schools and universities teach philosophy alongside theology on that basis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, infallibility, and how narrow it is. Your line was rarer than people think. The same council wrote a second document, and this one is about every thinking person.

Why is there something rather than nothing? The philosopher Leibniz asked it that way, but children ask it without the polish, sometimes at bedtime. Why is there a world? Who made the first thing? A tired parent might say, go to sleep. The First Vatican Council decided the question deserved a straight answer about what a human mind can and cannot reach on its own. Today's word is Dei Filius, Vatican One's document on faith and reason.
screen: `WHY IS THERE ANYTHING?` → `A BEDTIME QUESTION.` → `FAITH AND REASON.`

segments.voice: The council made three claims, and they fit together. First, reason can reach God. Dei Filius teaches that God, the beginning and end of all things, can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason, from the things he made. It takes that straight from Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." You don't need a Bible to wonder where the world came from, and the council says the wondering can actually get somewhere. Second, reason is not the whole road. God also revealed himself, so that the truths about him that reason could reach might be known by everyone, easily, firmly and without error mixed in. And there are mysteries hidden in God, the council says, that reason could never find alone; Catholics name the Trinity as one. Third, the two cannot truly fight. In its fourth chapter the council says there can never be a real disagreement between faith and reason, because the same God who reveals the mysteries gave the mind its light. If they seem to clash, either the faith has been misunderstood or an opinion has been mistaken for reason. Faith should help reason, and reason should help faith. So the council refused to say the mind is useless in religion, and refused to say the mind is enough.
screen: `REASON CAN REACH GOD.` · `REVELATION FILLS THE ROAD.` · `THEY CANNOT TRULY FIGHT.` · `NOT USELESS, NOT ENOUGH.` · then, large: `REASON REACHES TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing within reach, a cup, your own hand, the floor, and ask of it slowly: why is this here, and why is there anything to be here at all? Don't hurry to an answer; let the question stay open and see how far your mind goes with it. If you pray, let the question turn into thanks for the thing in front of you.
Dei Filius. The First Vatican Council's document teaching that faith and reason come from one God and can never truly contradict each other. Today's word.
Your line: reason reaches toward god. A hard question deserves a real thought. Day seven hundred eighty-nine, done.

790.title: Vatican II opens, 1962
790.hook: John XXIII calls a council to bring the Church up to date
790.howItsDone: Catholics remember the Second Vatican Council through its documents, read in parishes and schools, and the word aggiornamento is still used when describing how the Church presents its unchanging faith to each new age.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dei Filius: faith and reason come from one God. Your line was reason reaches toward god. The next council began with a surprise.

A new pope, and, the story goes, some expected him simply to keep the seat warm. A small group of cardinals in a Roman basilica, expecting a routine address. Then he tells them he means to call a council for the whole Church. The room, it's said, went quiet. The pope was John the Twenty-third, and the word that came to sum up what he wanted was Italian, his own language: aggiornamento.
screen: `A POPE TO KEEP THE SEAT WARM.` → `A COUNCIL FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.` → `AGGIORNAMENTO.`

segments.voice: Aggiornamento means bringing up to date. Not replacing, not starting over: updating, the way a family updates an old house it still loves. On the day the council opened, John the Twenty-third gave a speech known by its first Latin words, Gaudet Mater Ecclesia, Mother Church rejoices. Three things in it are worth carrying. First, he said he disagreed with the prophets of doom, people who could see nothing in the modern world but ruin. He wanted a council that looked at its own age with hope. Second, he drew a distinction that shaped everything after: the ancient teaching of the faith is one thing; the way it is put into words is another. The substance stays. The way of speaking can change, so that people today can actually hear it. That is aggiornamento in a sentence. Third, he said the Church today would rather use the medicine of mercy than of severity. Now the famous picture. People like to say he was asked what the council was for, walked to a window and threw it open, to let in fresh air. It's a story people tell. It isn't in the speech, and it may never have happened as told. But it stuck, because it pictured what he'd actually said. The Book of the Apocalypse, in the Douay-Rheims, has God say, "Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things: all things, new.
screen: `AGGIORNAMENTO: UP TO DATE.` · `NO PROPHETS OF DOOM.` · `SAME FAITH, NEW WORDS.` · `THE MEDICINE OF MERCY.` · then, large: `OPEN THE WINDOWS.`

segments.voice: If there's a window near you, open it, even a crack, or a door, or just turn toward the light, and notice the air coming in: its temperature, its smell, sounds that weren't in the room a minute ago. Nothing in the room has been thrown out; it's the same room, with air. If you pray, let the air carry a prayer for the Church.
Aggiornamento. Italian for bringing up to date: the same faith, put into words people today can hear. Today's word.
Your line: open the windows. Fresh air, without throwing out what you love. That's day seven hundred ninety.

791.title: The liturgy renewed (Sacrosanctum Concilium)
791.hook: full and active participation, and the Mass in the people's languages
791.tomorrow: The universal call to holiness (Lumen Gentium 5)
791.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics answer the priest's greetings, say or sing the Gloria, Creed, Holy and Lamb of God together, stand, sit and kneel at set moments, and keep silence at times; the Mass is celebrated in local languages and, in some places, in Latin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aggiornamento, and your line: open the windows. This week ran from the Vulgate and justification, through the seminaries, to Vatican One's two documents and the opening of Vatican Two. Today, the first window the council opened.

The priest says, The Lord be with you. And a whole church answers back, out loud, in the language they argue and shop and text in. It sounds so ordinary that it's easy to miss what a change it was. Some Catholics still remember Masses where the server gave the responses in Latin and the people prayed quietly on their own. The council's document on worship set out to change that. Today: the liturgy renewed.
screen: `THE LORD BE WITH YOU.` → `A WHOLE CHURCH ANSWERS.` → `THE LITURGY RENEWED.`

segments.voice: The document is called Sacrosanctum Concilium, from its first Latin words, this sacred council. Three ideas run through it. First, participation. The council said the Church earnestly desires that all the faithful be led to a full, conscious and active participation in the liturgy, and that this isn't a favor granted to them but their right and duty by baptism. It pointed to Saint Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation." The people at Mass are not an audience. Second, what taking part looks like. The council listed it: acclamations, responses, psalms, antiphons and songs, gestures and posture, and, at the proper times, a reverent silence. Silence counts. Kneeling counts. Third, language. Latin was to be kept in the Latin rites, and the mother tongue could be given a larger place, in the readings, the prayers and the chants, with the bishops deciding how. Catholics still differ over how far the changes should have gone, and some prefer the older form in Latin; the council's own text asked for both Latin and the people's languages to have a place. But the center of the document isn't the language question. It's the picture of a church where nobody is only watching. The psalm says it in the plural: "O magnify the Lord with me; and let us extol his name together."
screen: `FULL, CONSCIOUS, ACTIVE.` · `A KINGLY PRIESTHOOD.` · `SONG, GESTURE, AND SILENCE.` · `LATIN KEPT, MOTHER TONGUE WIDENED.` · then, large: `ALL OF US, TAKING PART.`

segments.voice: Bring one of the sung parts of Mass to mind, the Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lamb of God, the Alleluia, or simply And with your spirit, and hum it under your breath or just hear it inside. Notice where you'd usually go quiet. If you go to Mass, let that be the part you join next time, even softly; if you don't, think of one place in your week where you only watch, and could join.
Sacrosanctum Concilium. Vatican Two's document on worship, calling all the faithful to full, conscious and active participation in the liturgy. Today's word.
Your line: all of us, taking part. Nobody at Mass is only an audience. See you tomorrow.
